case_name: V.M. Gadre (Dead) By Lrs. And Ors. v M.G. Diwan And Others
petitioner: V.M. Gadre (Dead) By Lrs. And Ors
facts: The petitioners who are erstwhile Oriental employees and beneficiaries under the said Fund contend that the pension amount admissible under the said scheme is very meagre and, therefore, to ameliorate the conditions of the old and infirm pensioners it is necessary to revise the pension adequately, consistently with Arts. 38 and 39 of the Constitution.
The Oriental employees is a withering class.
Under the Pension-plan worked out for such employees, every employee had to contribute 5% of the substantive monthly salary and the employer had to make a matching grant every six months.
After the Act, the LIC took over the assets & properties of the erstwhile Company.
The pension was revised in 1980 and 1984 due to availability of funds in the Pension Fund but not by way of dearness increase, Efforts to seek increase in pension have since failed.

Since the cost of living was increasing by leaps and bounds the Oriental pensioners were finding it difficult to survive on their meagre pensions and hence they demanded increase in their pension amount by addition of dearness allowance as in the case of State and Central Government pensioners.
Their plight was even worse because their pensions had not been revised since 1954 and there was actually no increase in the dearness allowance on pensions since the last 33 years or thereabouts.
petitioner_arguments: The petitioners who are erstwhile Oriental employees and beneficiaries under the said Fund contend that the pension amount admissible under the said scheme is very meagre and, therefore, to ameliorate the conditions of the old and infirm pensioners it is necessary to revise the pension adequately, consistently with Arts. 38 and 39 of the Constitution.
The Oriental employees is a withering class.
Out of the pension paid to them, 6.38% is deducted every month to guarantee the payment of pension for ten years to the pensioners or their legal representatives.
Their main grievance was that there was no guarantee of pension and if they were to die, their legal representatives were granted only the residue of their contributions
To illustrate this, a short comparative chart has been set out in paragraph 11 of the counter affidavit.
respondent_arguments: After the insurance business was nationalized with effect from 1st September, 1956, u/s. 7 of the Act all assets and liabilities of existing insurers carrying on business in life insurance came to be transferred to and vested in the LIC.

The Pension Fund continued by it after its Constitution under the Act was in the nature of a contractual obligation and had to be governed strictly in accordance with the rules and regulations framed for its management.
Yet, however, it has to the extent possible under the rules and regulations governing the pension Fund given grants from time to time to ensure that the fund does not deplete.

The LIC contends that as at present under this Court's order the Oriental pensioners covered under the Fund are actually receiving more than the employees covered under the Provident Fund Scheme; any further increase will prompt the latter to demand that they too be covered under the said or similar pension scheme.
holding: The minimum pension is of Rs.375/- p.m. and the maximum pension is of Rs.1202.50/- p.m.

This Court should not exercise its jurisdiction u/art. 32 of the Constitution because the very same dispute was the subject matter of Writ Petition No.5137 of 1976 filed u/art. 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Bombay wherein the Court after considering the pros and cons of the demands made by Oriental employees rejected the same.
